Thermodynamic and economic comparison of pressure shift freezing and isochoric pressurization without a hyperbaric pump

# Boris Rubinsky · Alan Maida · Cristina Bilbao-Sainz

Received: 2 April 2026 / Accepted: 11 September 2026 This is a U.S. Government work and not under copyright protection in the US; foreign copyright protection may apply 2026

Abstract Pressure-assisted freezing produces frozen foods with finer ice crystals, less drip loss and longer microbiologi­ cal shelf life than conventional freezing, but its adoption has been limited because the conventional implemen­ tation, pressure-shift freezing (PSF), requires a hyperbaric pump delivering 100–200 MPa whose capital cost and mechanical complexity are the principal barrier to industrial deployment. A rigid constant-volume chamber cooled in a standard industrial freezer reaches the same pressurized subzero state passively, because partial ice formation in a confined volume drives the pressure along the ice Ih liquidus; this eliminates the pump at the cost of freezing sacrificial water, an overhead that grows with subzero depth. This work compares the two routes thermodynamically on an equal-output basis, from the ambient inlet state to the common pressurized subzero state that both must reach, with all water and ice properties evaluated from the IAPWS formulations. The two paths differ in a way that is thermodynamically fundamental: the PSF vessel is a moving-boundary system held at constant pressure by its pump, so its cooling duty is an enthalpy change and the pump must also supply boundary work as the fluid contracts, whereas the isochoric chamber is rigid, so its duty is an internalenergy change and no external work is supplied at all. Per kilogram of product delivered to the common state, isochoric pressurization consumes 53–87 kJ kg⁻¹ less electrical energy than batch PSF between − 5 and − 20 °C, and is competitive with an aspirational continuous flow-through PSF architecture above approximately − 9.4 °C. The crossover between the two routes is governed by the ratio of pumping to refrigeration efficiency rather than by either efficiency individually. Because the analysis stops at the shared state, the comparison is indepen­ dent of what is done downstream, and applies equally to isochoric preservation, in which the product is held unfrozen at that state, and to the hypothetical use of the isochoric chamber as a pressure generator for a subse­ quent decompression-nucleation step. The framework identifies batch operation, rather than the choice between mechanical and isochoric pressurization, as the dominant thermodynamic liability of conventional PSF.

## Introduction

Pressure-assisted freezing exploits the negative slope of the ice Ih–liquid coexistence curve: increasing pressure depresses the equilibrium freezing temperature of water, opening a thermodynamic window in which biologi­ cal materials can be held simultaneously at elevated pressure and subzero temperature1–3. When the pressure is subsequently released, the contents of the vessel are projected far below the atmospheric-pressure liquidus and rapidly nucleate ice throughout their bulk. The resulting ice microstructure is finer and more uniformly dis­ tributed than that produced by conventional surface-driven freezing. The benefit has been demonstrated across distinct product classes: in model gel systems, where matrix structure and rehydration behavior are improved4; in vegetable tissue, where potato cubes show improved texture, color and microstructure5; in fish and seafood, where salmon develops finer ice crystals than in classical freezing6 and smoked salmon mince shows microbial inactivation7; and in meat and marine products more generally8. The phenomenon and its thermodynamic basis are reviewed by LeBail and co-workers9 and by Li and Sun10, and the associated terminology is defined by Urru­ tia Benet and colleagues11.

An implementation of high pressure processing is pressure-shift freezing (PSF)12. In PSF a product is loaded into a rigid pressure vessel together with a transmitting fluid (typically water or a glycol mixture), pressurized by a hydraulic intensifier or plunger pump to 100–200 MPa, cooled to a subzero temperature while the contents remain liquid, and then rapidly decompressed. The amount of ice formed instantaneously on decompression has been quantified by Otero and Sanz13, and the resulting microstructure compared against high-pressure-assisted freezing by Fernández and co-workers14. The thermodynamic path is 1 → 2′ → 2 → 3 in Fig. 1A: ambient (1) → pressurization at room temperature (2′) → cooling at constant pressure to the target state (2) → atmospheric supercooling and nucleation (3). Despite the documented product-quality advantages6,15,16, PSF has not achieved widespread industrial deployment in food preservation. Hyperbaric intensifiers, dynamic high-pressure seals, and the autofrettage or composite-overwrap vessels that house them represent a multi-million-dollar capital expenditure and operate as a batch process that further penalises throughput.

Isochoric freezing-driven pressurization (IFP) offers a thermodynamically distinct route to the same pres­ surized liquid–ice equilibrium without an external pressurizing pump. The physical principles are reviewed by Consiglio and co-workers22, the temperature–volume phase behavior is mapped by Powell-Palm23,28, and the multiphase thermodynamic theory has been validated experimentally1,23. A rigid, constant-volume chamber is filled with the product and an aqueous medium and cooled in a standard industrial freezer. Because ice Ih is less dense than liquid water, partial ice formation in a confined volume forces the system pressure to rise along the liquidus curve until thermal equilibrium is reached at the freezer setpoint. The thermodynamic path is 1 → 2” → 2→ 3 in Fig. 1A. Our experiments show that the sealing temperature of the isochoric chamber strongly affects the freezing process. Water expands as it warms above freezing. Therefore, the sealing temperature changes the cooling path inside the chamber. The internal pressure and ice fraction are uniquely determined by the tempera­ ture and by the state at which the chamber was sealed. Therefore, in our experiments we systematically seal the chamber at 0 °C. Starting from 0 °C, the isochoric freezing process follows the liquidus line (Fig. 1B); at − 20 °C the internal pressure reaches 194 MPa with an ice fraction of 0.55. From a capital-cost perspective, IFP replaces the hyperbaric pump, intensifier, dynamic seals and high-cycle pressure vessel of PSF with a static rigid container cooled by ordinary industrial refrigeration. The price of this simplification is a thermodynamic one: a fraction φ of the water in the chamber must be frozen to generate the pressure, so to deliver one kilogram of unfrozen pressurized liquid at state 2 the system must process a total of 1/(1 − φ) ≥ 1 kg of mass. The corresponding massscaling factor r = 1/(1 − φ) rises from 1.34 at − 5 °C to 2.22 at − 20 °C.

Although PSF and isochoric freezing have each been studied extensively, prior work has concentrated on product quality, microbial inactivation, and process phenomenology. Isochoric freezing has been reviewed as an emerging preservation technology24–27, its instrumentation and physicochemical influence surveyed28, and its application demonstrated for chicken breast29,30, orange and carot juice31,32, milk33, a range of horticultural products34–37, microbial and spore inactivation38–41. A rigorous thermodynamic comparison of the two pressur­ ization strategies on an equal-output basis, quantifying the energetic price of the IFP sacrificial freezing against the energetic price of the PSF decompression event at a common end state, has not previously been established. The economic framing of the choice between the two technologies has therefore rested on capital-cost arguments alone, without an underlying physical accounting of the recurring operating-energy cost in either direction.

The present work develops a common thermodynamic framework for comparing the two routes on an equaloutput basis. The contribution is fivefold. First, all thermophysical properties are taken directly from the IAPWS formulations, so that no constant specific heat, constant latent heat or constant specific volume enters the energy or exergy balance. Second, the minimum freezing exergy required to produce one kilogram of useful frozen product is derived explicitly from first principles, providing a reversible benchmark independent of equipment choices. Third, the cycle-level pressurization efficiency of batch PSF is derived bottom-up from the componentlevel plunger-pump efficiency, making the decompression-loss term falsifiable and traceable to a standard hard­ ware specification. Fourth, a three-way comparison of batch PSF, continuous flow-through processing and IFP is conducted over − 5 to − 20 °C. Fifth, a sensitivity analysis establishes the structural result that the crossover between IFP and flow-through PSF depends on the two equipment efficiencies only through their ratio. The central question is operational and economic: when does eliminating the hyperbaric pump in favor of sacrificial isochoric freezing produce a net reduction in operating-energy cost per kilogram of useful frozen product, and when does it not?

## Methods

Scope and assumptions

The analysis is a cycle-level thermodynamic comparison between two pressure-generation strategies at an equiv­ alent processing endpoint. The following assumptions are adopted throughout and applied uniformly to both PSF and IFP.

i. Quasi-equilibrium operation: each process is treated as a sequence of equilibrium states along its ther­ modynamic path. Transient thermal gradients, finite cooling rates, and finite decompression rates are not modeled. This is a modeling choice of the present work rather than an established convention, and its consequences are examined in Sect. 5.5. ii. Negligible nucleation kinetics and crystal-morphology effects on the energy balance: ice nucleation and crystal growth are essential to the product-quality argument for pressure-assisted freezing but do not enter the first-law or second-law balance per kilogram of frozen product. The kinetics of instantaneous ice formation on decompression are treated separately in the literature13. iii. Negligible vessel wall heat capacity, ancillary thermal mass, and product non-aqueous heat capacity: the refrigeration duty is computed for the water content of the system. The asymmetry this introduces between the two routes is quantified in Sect. 5.5. iv. The pressure-transmitting medium in PSF is water, and the pressurizing pump is a positive-displacement plunger/intensifier whose component-level mechanical efficiency is in the range of in line-eq-IEq1 ≈ 0.8542,43. The cycle-level effectiveness of this pump under batch operation is derived in Sect. 2.7 rather than assumed, in the manner of the audit of Atuonwu and Tassou20. v. The refrigeration plant is shared between PSF and IFP: a single industrial cascade refrigeration system delivers cold to either process, and its temperature-dependent coefficient of performance is computed from the Carnot limit with a fixed second-law efficiency factor44,45.

Under these assumptions the comparison is a thermodynamic equivalence in the sense of equal output mass at equal end state, not a claim of identical kinetics, microstructure, or product quality. The product-quality implica­ tions are discussed in Sect.  5.4.

Where the comparison begins and ends

Both routes start at state A, product and water at ambient temperature and atmospheric pressure, and both must reach state 2, the target subzero temperature T at the corresponding liquidus pressure p(T). The paths between these states differ, and the present analysis is confined to that difference. In PSF the charge is pressurized at ambient temperature (step B) and then cooled under pressure to the target temperature (step C). In the isochoric route the charge is cooled to 0 °C at atmospheric pressure (step B) and then cooled further within the sealed rigid chamber, where progressive ice formation raises the pressure along the liquidus until the target state is reached (step C).

Everything downstream of state 2 is common to the two routes and cancels. In pressure-shift freezing the pres­ sure is released, the supercooled liquid nucleates throughout its bulk, the latent heat released returns the product to approximately 0 °C, and the partially frozen product is then cooled to its storage temperature at atmospheric pressure. That sequence is identical whether state 2 was reached mechanically or isochorically, and modeling it would add the same quantity to both sides of the comparison. Restricting the analysis to steps B and C therefore removes a large common term without loss of generality.

It also confines the comparison to processes that have been demonstrated, which requires care to state pre­ cisely. Isochoric preservation as practiced to date does not proceed beyond state 2: the product is held unfro­ zen within the unfrozen fraction at the temperature and pressure of that state, and the chamber is subsequently

Cycle-level pressurization efficiency for batch PSF

The single most consequential modeling choice in comparing PSF to IFP is the pressurization efficiency assigned to the PSF pumping system, because pump electrical energy is exactly the cost that IFP avoids. We distinguish a component-level efficiency in line-eq-IEq35, the steady-state head efficiency of the pressurizing device operating continu­ ously, taken here as 0.85, a value assumed rather than measured and lying within the range typical of reciprocat­ ing positive-displacement pumps; the sensitivity analysis of Sect.  4.4 shows that the comparison depends on this quantity only through its ratio to the refrigeration efficiency, which is why an assumed value is tolerable, from a cycle-level effectiveness, the fraction of electrical energy drawn by the entire pressurizing subsystem that appears as net useful pressure work on the product over a complete batch pressurize–hold–decompress cycle.

For a single-vessel batch installation, three mechanisms reduce the cycle-level effectiveness. (a) Decompres­ sion energy loss: at the end of every cycle the pressurized fluid is vented, and the elastic energy stored in the compressed water, equal in magnitude to Wp, is dissipated irreversibly. (b) Water compressibility: the additional fluid displaced by compression must also be pumped, and that work is likewise lost on decompression. (c) Idle and ancillary loads during the hold phase. A model-based analysis of industrial high-pressure processing equip­ ment, validated against three instrumented case studies, defines an effectiveness factor as the ratio of compression electrical energy to the total electrical energy consumed per cycle, and reports measured values of 0.44, 0.46 and 0.8220. ## Discussion

Batch versus continuous operation: the dominant variable

The most striking finding of the three-way comparison is that the difference between batch PSF and flow-through PSF, both of which use mechanical pressurization, is consistently larger than the difference between mechanical and isochoric pressurization at fixed operating mode. At − 15 °C the batch-versus-flow-through energy difference is 125 kJ kg⁻¹, while the flow-through-versus-isochoric difference is 41 kJ kg⁻¹. The dominant thermodynamic liability of PSF as currently practiced is the irrecoverable decompression event at the end of every batch cycle, not the use of a mechanical pump per se. This has two consequences. First, attention paid to mechanical energy recovery addresses a larger fraction of the PSF inefficiency than improvements in pump head efficiency alone. Second, a comparison of PSF and IFP that uses the steady-state plunger-pump efficiency of 0.85 for PSF, as is sometimes done, is thermodynamically inconsistent for a batch process and substantially understates the energy cost of PSF as actually operated. Equations (11) and (12) provide an explicit, falsifiable correction.

Combining the operating-energy comparison with the capital-cost argument, three regimes emerge. (i) At tar­ get temperatures above approximately − 10 °C, IFP is energetically equivalent to, or modestly preferable to, even an idealized flow-through PSF system that does not currently exist commercially; because IFP addition­ ally eliminates the hyperbaric-pump capital expenditure, it dominates PSF on every axis in this regime. (ii) Between approximately − 10 and − 15 °C, IFP remains competitive with idealized flow-through PSF and retains an 84–87 kJ kg⁻¹ energy advantage over the real industrial alternative, batch PSF, while its exergy advantage passes through zero near − 11.7 °C. (iii) Below approximately − 15 °C, the sacrificial-freezing penalty grows large enough that an idealized flow-through system would be preferred if available; in its absence IFP remains prefer­ able to batch PSF on energy grounds but loses on exergy grounds.

Which route is preferred for a given application therefore turns on a single quantity: the target temperature at state 2 that the application requires. That target is set by the intended downstream use, and it should not be confused with the storage temperature of the finished product, which is reached later by conventional means and lies outside the present comparison. Wherever the required state-2 temperature is milder than the crossover, the isochoric route is preferred against every PSF architecture considered here; for colder targets it remains preferred against the batch equipment that is actually available, though an idealized continuous system would be better still. Because the crossover lies at − 9.4 °C under the most conservative assumption and moves below − 20 °C at the filling efficiencies specified for commercial vessels, the isochoric route is preferred across most of the range examined. A processor evaluating the two technologies should locate the crossover for their own plant from the efficiency ratio of Eq. (14) rather than adopt the generic value quoted here.

Beyond state 2: product quality

Because the comparison terminates at state 2, product quality lies outside it. Two observations are nonetheless worth recording. First, the two routes deliver different chamber contents at that state: a PSF vessel holds the product in liquid transmitting fluid, whereas an isochoric chamber holds it among inl i ne -eq-IEq93= 25–55% ice. Whether that ice acts as a thermal reservoir favorable to subsequent nucleation, or as a mechanical constraint on delicate structures, is an empirical question this framework cannot resolve; it is sharpest at deep temperatures, where the ice fraction is largest, and mildest in the superchilling window where the isochoric route is most favored. Dual-compartment designs that isolate the product within the liquid fraction are the natural response and merit dedicated study. Second, adiabatic decompression cools the contents by approximately 2–3 °C per 100 MPa55, identical for both routes at equal state 2, and therefore absent from the comparison.

Practical deviations from the idealized assumptions

The assumptions of Sect.  2.1 are applied uniformly to both routes, but uniform application does not by itself guarantee that the comparison is unaffected: what matters is whether the deviation from each assumption in a real installation is symmetric between PSF and IFP. We consider each in turn and identify those that are not.

Product composition

Real foods are 70–90% water, with lower specific heat and lower latent heat per kilogram than pure water, so the refrigeration duty of both routes falls by a similar factor. Because inline-eq-IEq94 is a property of the pressure-generating water in the chamber rather than of the product, the mass-scaling factor is unchanged. The deviation is therefore close to neutral: absolute energies fall for both routes, differences scale approximately in proportion, and the crossover moves little. Solutes do depress the freezing point and modify the liquidus, which is the effect covered by the ± 10% ice-fraction sensitivity of Sect.  4.4.

Vessel thermal mass

This deviation is not symmetric, and it acts against IFP. Both routes require a vessel rated for 100–200 MPa, but the IFP chamber must contain inline-eq-IEq95kilograms of water per kilogram of useful product and is correspondingly larger, so its wall mass per kilogram of product is greater by roughly the same factor. Since the chamber is cooled and rewarmed on each cycle, its heat capacity enters the refrigeration duty directly. For a steel chamber of practical wall thickness the parasitic duty is of the order of several per cent of the water duty per cycle, so the IFP penalty relative to PSF is a few per cent of inline-eq-IEq96 — small compared with the 53–87 kJ kg⁻¹ advantage, but a genuine erosion of it that grows with r and therefore with subzero depth.

Quasi-equilibrium operation and cycle time

This deviation is also asymmetric against IFP. Cooling inline-eq-IEq97kilograms through a conduction-limited path takes lon­ ger than cooling one, so the IFP cycle is longer at fixed refrigeration capacity and accumulates more heat leak per kilogram of product. The energy effect is modest for a well-insulated chamber; the throughput effect is not, and is treated in Sect.  5.6. Transient gradients also mean that a real chamber is never exactly at the uniform state assumed in Eq. (2); the local ice fraction varies through the chamber, and the reported r should be read as a chamber average.

Idealized pressurization

The deviations here act against PSF. Real high-pressure systems lose fluid through dynamic seals, and leakage must be made up by additional pumping work that is entirely lost. Intensifiers operate off their design point during much of the pressurization ramp, so the effective head efficiency is below nameplate. Both effects reduce the true cycle effectiveness below the 0.46 of Eq. (11), which is why the measured audit range extends down to 0.4420. IFP has no analogue of either loss, having no dynamic seal and no pump. The idealization is therefore conservative with respect to the present conclusion rather than favorable to it.

Shared refrigeration plant

The assumption that a single plant serves either process is reasonable at equal target temperature, but a real IFP installation places a larger and more sustained load on the plant, since it must remove r times the latent heat over

Non-energy implementation considerations

Operating energy and equipment capital cost are the two terms the present framework quantifies, but they are not the only terms that determine adoption. Several considerations fall outside the thermodynamic analysis, and they do not all favor the same route.

Maintenance

The dominant consumable-maintenance item in high-pressure food processing is the dynamic high-pressure seal, subject to wear and periodic replacement at intervals set by cycle count, together with the intensifier packing and the associated hydraulic circuit. IFP has no dynamic high-pressure seal and no pump: the chamber closure is a static seal opened and closed at atmospheric pressure and never exposed to sliding contact under load. This removes an entire maintenance category rather than reducing it, and is a substantial part of the practical case for IFP, distinct from the avoided capital cost of the pump itself.

Operational complexity and safety

A PSF installation requires an intensifier skid, hydraulic utilities, high-pressure tubing runs, and the operator training and periodic inspection that pressure equipment attracts under ASME Section VIII or the European Pressure Equipment Directive. An IFP chamber is also a pressure component and remains subject to design and inspection requirements, but it is a sealed vessel with no external pressure circuit, no pressurized lines outside the chamber, and no active pressurization to control; the pressure is a consequence of temperature and is bounded by it, which simplifies both the control system and the failure analysis.

Throughput and cycle time

This consideration works against IFP and is not captured by the per-kilogram energy balance. Because the cham­ ber must cool inline-eq-IEq98kilograms of water per kilogram of useful product, and cooling is conduction-limited, the cycle time at fixed refrigeration capacity scales approximately with inline-eq-IEq99, from about 1.3 times the equivalent PSF freezing time at − 5 °C to about 2.2 times at − 20 °C. Where a line is throughput-limited rather than energy-limited this penalty may dominate the operating-energy advantage entirely, and it must be evaluated per installation. It can be mitigated by chamber geometry that shortens the conduction path, at the cost of a lower ratio of product to chamber wall.

Scalability

The cost of a high-pressure vessel rises steeply with both volume and design pressure, so PSF scales by enlarg­ ing a single expensive vessel and its intensifier. IFP scales by replicating chambers in parallel within a freezer, so capacity is added in small increments with a nearly linear cost and no single point of failure. The counterpart

IFP chambers are cooled by ordinary industrial refrigeration and can in principle be loaded into existing blast freezers, plate freezers or cold rooms, offering an incremental retrofit path within existing plant and existing cold-chain logistics. PSF requires a dedicated high-pressure bay with its own utilities and is difficult to introduce incrementally. For a processor evaluating pressure-assisted freezing for the first time, the availability of a lowcommitment pilot within existing infrastructure is a considerable practical advantage of IFP that is independent of the thermodynamic comparison.

Taken together, these considerations reinforce the energy-based case for IFP in the mild-freezing window and partially offset its energy disadvantage at deep temperatures, with the important exception of throughput, which works against IFP at every temperature and increasingly so with subzero depth.

## Conclusions

A common thermodynamic framework was developed to compare two routes to pressure-assisted freezing of foods on an equal-output basis: conventional pressure-shift freezing, which uses a hydraulic pump to deliver 100–200 MPa to a batch processing vessel, and isochoric freezing-driven pressurization, which generates the same pressure passively by partial isochoric freezing of additional water in a rigid container cooled by standard industrial refrigeration. All thermophysical properties were evaluated from the IAPWS formulations, so that the comparison rests on reference equations of state rather than on constant-property approximations. The framework quantifies the recurring operating-energy cost of substituting sacrificial freezing for a hyperbaric pump, the cen­ tral economic trade-off that has so far been argued in capital-cost terms alone.

Under a cycle-level pressurization efficiency derived from the component-level plunger-pump efficiency and accounting for the irrecoverable decompression event at the end of every PSF batch cycle, the isochoric route consumes 53–87 kJ kg⁻¹ less electrical energy than batch PSF across the − 5 to − 20 °C range at the conserva­ tive filling efficiency FE = 1, and far more at realistic filling efficiencies. Against an idealized flow-through PSF system that does not currently exist commercially, IFP is energetically equivalent above approximately − 10 °C and inferior by 3–103 kJ kg⁻¹ at lower temperatures, the latter penalty arising from the mass-scaling factor r = 1/ (1 − φ) intrinsic to isochoric pressurization. The exergy destruction follows the same qualitative pattern with a crossover near − 11.7 °C.

The sensitivity analysis shows that the crossover between IFP and flow-through PSF is governed by the ratio of pumping to refrigeration efficiency rather than by either efficiency individually, and lies between approxi­ mately − 4 °C and − 15 °C over the full plausible parameter range with a baseline near − 10 °C. The energy advantage of IFP over batch PSF is preserved throughout the − 5 to − 15 °C window across every parameter com­ bination tested, and is preserved across the entire tested envelope, and widens substantially once the pressuretransmitting mass of the PSF vessel is accounted for.

The three-way comparison identifies batch operation, rather than the choice between mechanical and isochoric pressurization, as the dominant thermodynamic liability of conventional PSF. Equivalently, the operating-energy cost of eliminating the hyperbaric pump in favor of sacrificial isochoric freezing is small or favorable across the temperature range of practical interest for frozen-food processing. The framework provides a basis for technol­ ogy selection that complements the capital-cost argument by quantifying the recurring operating-energy term, and it locates that basis precisely: the crossover near − 9.4 °C lies above the − 18 °C retail frozen-storage stan­ dard, so IFP is unambiguously preferred in the superchilling and mild-freezing window while, in the deep-freeze

window, it is an improvement on the available pressure-assisted alternative rather than the thermodynamically optimal route.

Five challenges remain before either route can be committed to industrial adoption. First, no instrumented energy audit of a complete installation of either route at food-processing scale has been reported, so the cyclelevel effectiveness of Eqs. (11) and (12) and the sensitivity envelopes of Sect.  4.4 remain modeled rather than measured; such audits are the highest-priority validation step. Second, published isochoric work is conducted at laboratory chamber volumes, and demonstration at food-processing scale is required before the throughput and thermal-mass penalties of Sect.  5.5 and 5.6 can be quantified rather than estimated. Third, the effect on prod­ uct quality of the 25–55% ice fraction present in an IFP chamber before decompression is unresolved and must be characterized experimentally for each product class against the well-documented PSF benchmarks. Fourth, chamber geometry and fill protocol have not been optimized; reducing the effective mass-scaling factor below its thermodynamic bound through displacement fixtures, dual-compartment designs, or pre-chilled sealing would directly reduce the principal energy penalty of IFP. Fifth, pressure-assisted freezing as a novel process requires validation against food-safety regulatory frameworks, which for processes of this kind is frequently the ratelimiting step regardless of the thermodynamic case. The framework developed here is intended to inform where that effort is best directed, not to substitute for it.
